content: In 2009, outcomes for children with a mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) of less than 115 mm were reported. A study by Manary in 2004, conducted in Malawi, involved 282 children in a non-randomized controlled comparative trial. The children were treated with ready-to-use therapeutic food (RUTF) and compared across three home-based dietary groups. The first group received RUTF in quantities sufficient to meet their full nutrient requirements for catch-up growth (733 kJ/kg/day or 175 kcal/kg/day). The second group was given a multivitamin/mineral-fortified RUTF supplement providing 2090 kJ/day, which accounted for approximately 33% (ranging from 25% to 50%) of their daily energy needs. The third group received maize/soy flour. The study reported that children achieved weight-for-height z-scores (WHZ) greater than -2 and resolved edema after eight weeks of therapy. In another study by Oakley in 2010, also conducted in Malawi, 1874 children aged 6–59 months were enrolled in a double-blind randomized controlled trial. The trial compared two RUTF formulations: one containing 25% milk (n=954) and another with 15% milk (n=929). The primary outcome was achieving a WHZ greater than -2 and no edema after eight weeks of outpatient therapy. The group receiving the 25% milk RUTF showed better recovery outcomes. These children were treated as inpatients for 3–4 weeks with a diet providing 180 kcal/kg/day and 4 g protein/kg/day. The study reported weight gain and resolution of diarrhea in most cases. Approximately 75% of the population overlapped with children who had edema, which was treated exclusively in outpatient settings. Outcomes for children with WHZ scores below -3 were also reported in various studies. For example, weight and MUAC gains were assessed at four weeks in most studies, except for Bekele (2009) and Oakley (2010), where assessments were conducted at eight weeks. Recovery rates were expressed as persons per 1000 person-days, with some children still under treatment at the end of the study period. Several studies were excluded from analysis due to various reasons, such as focusing on disease treatment rather than severe malnutrition, lack of MUAC-based admission or follow-up data, or failure to report nutritional rehabilitation outcomes. For instance, Akinbami (2010) and Bejon (2008) focused on disease treatment in hospitalized children, while Beckett (2000) included children with moderate malnutrition rather than severe cases. Other studies, such as Collins (2006) and Manary (2008), were general reviews or position papers on malnutrition management without specific MUAC-related outcomes. The World Health Organization (WHO) and other organizations have emphasized the importance of MUAC as a reliable indicator for identifying and managing severe acute malnutrition (SAM) in children. Studies have demonstrated the utility of MUAC in community-based therapeutic care programs and its correlation with other anthropometric indicators like weight-for-height z-scores.
